exchanges.question: What drove the improvement in the current accident year loss ratio versus 2Q 2025, which differs from what other commercial insurers are reporting (lower non-cat property losses, mix, changes in loss picks)? Second, the ceding commission rate has been rising for a couple of years; is the same expected this year after the reinsurance renewals?
exchanges.answer: Allibhai said losses came in below expectations as they have for the last few quarters, with nothing out of the ordinary, just normal variability and mix across a composite of a dozen statutory lines, and reserves are as conservative as they have ever been. Petrucelli said the second quarter is a good indication of the expense ratio going forward, with a slight uptick possible in the net commission ratio; reinsurance treaties renewed June 1st so only one month of the new treaty is reflected, and AI-driven efficiency gains on the operating side could offset, so in aggregate the Q2 expense ratio is a good measure going forward.

exchanges.question: With E&S casualty softening and GWP up about 3% versus 4% in Q1, how much are ROEs compressing in that line assuming loss trend views of high single digits to low double digits are unchanged? Second, how is Kinsale thinking about broker commissions going forward, given brokers push for higher commissions in soft markets and appear to be placing more business on the admitted side?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe said everything is managed to a 20% ROE or greater, most product lines are probably running ahead of that, and the company produced 24.4% for the quarter, with a constant give and take between profit and growth. On brokers, he said there is normal tension between wholesalers and retailers over splitting the gross commission, which a soft market intensifies, but Kinsale offers the best customer service, quote ratio, response time and broadest risk appetite in the industry and continues to grow outside the Commercial Property Division, which is going through a unique correction.

exchanges.question: Is 2Q the trough for commercial property given larger players are pulling out, and could pricing become less negative in 2027 or Kinsale return to larger shared placements? Second, what is driving the 3.7% ex-property growth figure, is business returning to the admitted market, and what would need to change for that number to inflect?
exchanges.answer: Winston said there is no telling where property goes in 2027; pressure continues from MGAs in London and traditional markets remain heavy in shared and layered deals with larger limits and stretch primaries, so Kinsale will keep pricing tactical, meet return thresholds and accept shrinking in that division. On ex-property growth, heavy competition in long-tail lines from London is creeping into other liability occurrence lines and depressing Construction pricing, with more competition emerging in general casualty, but there are pockets of opportunity to lean into. There is some flow to the admitted market but it is not pervasive.

exchanges.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts cited in the press release comes from broker engagement versus more competitive pricing? Second, what is the current view of social inflation and casualty loss cost trend, and was the favorable accident year variability entirely in short-tail property?
exchanges.answer: Winston said it is a bit of both: the idle broker initiative to reengage lapsed brokers is increasing flow, hit ratios on renewal and new business are roughly unchanged, and more submissions mean more accounts bind. Kehoe added the language was included to show confidence in the model, since the Commercial Property crisis is over and rates are coming down dramatically but the underlying business is still working well. Allibhai put casualty loss cost trend at probably mid-single digits varying by line, said smaller accounts and lower limits leave Kinsale less exposed to social inflation, and said favorable losses are across the board with short-tail lines performing especially well. Kehoe added that for a couple of years the company has slowed the release of IBNR in longer-tail occurrence business while letting it flow out more quickly in short-tail lines.

exchanges.question: What granularity can be given on property pricing in Q2 versus Q1, and when might pricing reach equilibrium? Second, with the mix shifting from property to casualty, should the underlying current accident year loss ratio drift up or is the level sustainable? Third, how should the pacing of buybacks be thought about going forward if top-line growth remains moderate?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe said equilibrium will eventually come because catastrophe losses do happen, but the company has no insight into when; other property divisions are seeing growth. Winston cited Agribusiness Property and small business property as more stable than large shared and layered deals over the last year and a half to two years, noted a little more competition in Inland Marine across its five product buckets, and said people are starting to reach the floor on property pricing though London pressure persists. Allibhai said the accident year loss ratio could drift up over time but losses are coming in below expectations and they feel good about current bookings, and Kehoe added IBNR conservatism is a positive indicator. On buybacks, Kehoe said they will continue to lean in: the first $100 million authorization was exhausted a little over a year ago, roughly $80 million remains on the subsequent $250 million, plus the new $250 million; buybacks are the principal capital allocation strategy alongside a small dividend, with growth becoming first priority again when it accelerates.

exchanges.question: How has product expansion contributed to growth over the past year, and what is the potential growth uplift from the new products going forward?
exchanges.answer: Winston said Kinsale never wants to jump into a new market feet first and grow like a weed; new products follow a crawl, walk, run pace. They are creating growth and driving submissions and new premium, but growth will be slow, ramping up as the market turns.
